newsitem.title: UK: Britain ready to sign EU workers' rights pact.
newsitem.headline: Britain ready to sign EU workers' rights pact.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Monday it would take the first step towards signing the European Union's Social Chapter, set up to regulate working conditions throughout the 15-nation bloc.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, appointed after Labour's landslide victory in Britain's May 1 election, said the move would come at a meeting in Brussels on Monday forming part of the EU's rolling Intergovernmental Conference (IGC).
"At today's meeting Britain will take the first step towards signing up to the Social Chapter," Cook said in a statement.
"We will tell our European partners that we want the rights and benefits of the Social Chapter to extend to the people of Britain."

The ousted Conservative government of John Major had opposed signing the Social Chapter, saying the regulations would make Britain less able to compete with other countries and could cost up to 500,000 jobs.
Labour made signing the Social Chapter -- under which new parents are granted three months unpaid leave and large multinational firms have to consult their workers -- an election campaign pledge.
"We do not accept that the British people should be second-class citizens with less rights than employees on the continent," Cook said.
"Today's meeting opens a new chapter in Britain's relations with Europe," Cook said. "It marks a fresh start in Europe for Britain, working with other member states as a partner, not as an opponent."
The meeting on Monday and Tuesday will allow Britain's newly appointed Minister for Europe, Doug Henderson, to set out the Labour government's approach to the IGC.

Cook said: "The British people have demanded to share in the benefits of the Social Chapter in repeated opinion polls. Today's initiative is a democratic response to the wishes of the British people."
Cook made clear in an interview published on Sunday that he expected Britain to sign the Social Chapter within a month.

In comments signalling a desire to improve relations with Europe after distinct frostiness under the Conservatives -- particularly as a result of the mad cow crisis -- Cook told Sunday's Observer newspaper that Britain would shun xenophobia.
However, he said Britain was still unlikely to join the planned European single currency in the first wave in 1999.
"We want to take Britain back out of a position of isolation, out of inward-looking chauvinism and into being a leading member of an international community," he told the newspaper.
"Personally, I think we are entering a period when international politics is coming of age."
